Eyes (20-20-20)

Regular eye breaks while looking at screens.

The 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet (6 metres) away for at least 20 seconds. It gives your eye's focusing muscles a rest from close-up screen work.
  • Reduces digital eye strain, dryness and blurry vision
  • Cuts down on headaches from prolonged screen focus
  • Encourages a natural blink reset, which re-moistens the eyes
Remind every 20 min

Walk

Short movement breaks to counter prolonged sitting.

2–5 minute movement breaks: stand up, stretch, or take a short walk every so often — even a lap around the room counts.
  • Improves blood circulation and reduces stiffness
  • Counters the posture strain of prolonged sitting
  • Gives a small energy and focus boost for the next stretch of work
Remind every 45 min
Sound

WalkTime for a 2–5 minute walk or stretch!

Water

Stay on top of hydration through the day.

How much to drink: aim for roughly 200–250ml (a glass) at each reminder — that works out to about 2–3 litres across a day for most adults, adjusted for activity level and climate.
  • Supports concentration and energy — even mild dehydration affects focus
  • Helps digestion and keeps skin and joints healthier
  • Small, frequent sips are easier on the body than drinking a lot at once
Remind every 60 min

Eyes (Exercise)

Guided eye exercise: the moving dot cycles through seven patterns — zigzag, figure-8, loop, star, cross, and a row scan — directions your eyes rarely get from a fixed screen.
  • Max 2 sessions a day — one in the morning to wake up focus, one in the evening after screen work
  • Each session is exactly 2:15 — don't repeat it back-to-back; over-exercising can cause tension headaches or eye strain
  • Aim for 3–5 days a week — resting the other days prevents ciliary muscle fatigue and focus cramping

Wake-Up Time

3:00 – 4:30 AM is far earlier than the body's natural rhythm and usually cuts sleep short — red zone.
4:30 – 5:30 AM works for early risers used to it, but can still shorten sleep for most people — orange zone.
5:30 – 6:30 AM lines up well with most people's natural cortisol rhythm and gives a calm morning before the day's demands start — green zone, the sweet spot.
6:30 – 7:30 AM is still a perfectly healthy, common wake time — orange-green.
7:30 – 9:00 AM tends to compress the rest of the day's routine into a shorter window — orange zone.
Every activity below shifts automatically with whatever you pick here, and the Sleep time is always set to give at least 8 hours before the next wake-up.

☀️ Morning

The warmth and gentle pressure relaxes the eye muscles and improves blood flow after hours of closed-eye rest, easing the eyes into the day rather than opening straight into bright light or a screen.
Rehydrates the body after the overnight fast, kick-starts digestion, and helps flush out toxins — your body loses water through breathing and sweat even while asleep.

🌙 Evening & Night

🌅

Rise & Reset

  • Morning mood is a teaser of the day. The decision is yours as to how the main picture should be.
  • Have a bath — wash off yesterday's dirt and let its thoughts rinse away.
  • Leave yesterday in yesterday — don't copy-paste it into today.
  • 0 expectations = ∞ happiness.
🚦

Traffic Therapy

  • Just think whether your reaction is worth it.
  • You are more valuable than your vehicle. So are others.
  • Be patient or become a patient.
💪

Work on Yourself

  • Learning something new for a few minutes a day brings returns with compound interest.
  • Mistakes aren't charity. Don't donate yours to others. Accept them.
  • Take criticism like a vaccine — brief sting, lasting immunity.
  • Jealousy makes you less. Put up a "No Entry" sign.
🌙

Sign-Off

  • The best medicine is sleep.
  • The side effect of thoughts in bed is sleeplessness.
  • Couldn't control your thoughts? Tonight's thought seeds are the next morning's harvest. So, choose what you sow.

Privacy Policy

Body & Activity section: The exercise and yoga recommendations are general fitness guidance based on the age group you select. No personal health information, biometric data, or activity history is collected, stored, or transmitted to any server — all calculations happen locally in your browser.

Food & Nutrition section: The dietary preference and age group you choose to generate nutrition suggestions are used only to compute recommendations within your current browser session. This information is not saved, logged, or shared with us or any third party.

Feedback: If you submit feedback, the name and message you provide are sent to us for review. Please avoid including sensitive personal or medical information in your feedback.

Advertising: This site displays advertisements, which may be served by third-party ad networks. These networks may use cookies, device identifiers, or similar technologies to show ads, measure their performance, and limit how often you see the same ad. This may include information about your general location, device type, and browsing activity on this site. We do not control how third-party ad networks use this data — please refer to their own privacy policies for details. You can manage or block ad-related data collection through your browser's cookie and privacy settings.

Cookies

This site uses two kinds of local storage (cookies and similar browser storage):

Necessary Remembers things like your age group, diet selection, and reminder settings on this device. The app doesn't work properly without these, so they're always on.
Advertising Loads Google AdSense, which may set cookies to show and measure ads. If this is off, the ad script isn't loaded at all.

Notification Settings

The Alerts tab (Break / Walk / Drink reminders) can send you a browser notification when it's time — a popup in your taskbar on desktop, or a system notification on mobile. This needs your browser's permission first.
